comments: I already have a recent master's in Writing Studies and Educational Psychology with a 4.0 GPA, as well as over a decade of social work experience, and several academic publications, conference presentations, and workshops that focused on therapeutic techniques, mental wellbeing, or disability. I also taught for my entire master's degree, was an Assistant Director of the Writing Center, and conducted my own 100+ participant study. I was waitlisted on March 30th, told all decisions would be final by April 24th, and then received an email offering me admission into the part-time and non-funded 3-year program (rather than the full-time, funded 2-year program I had applied for) on April 29th. I was told within the next week I would get my official offer of admission, and I had that same one week to accept it and pay the $250 admission fee. I emailed back 6 days later saying I had discussed with my support network and had decided to reject the offer due to national instability and uncertainty of gov financial aid, but would like to reapply in the future. I asked how to indicate this acceptance on a potential future application, as I had never received an official admission offer. Two weeks after that, I got my official admission offer and a host of emails telling me what my next steps were. All of them had inconsistent and contradictory information, including dates that were different email to email and deadlines that had passed weeks ago. One email had three different dates for the same (important) deadline. comments: Early Nov 2025 contacted potential supervisor and was encouraged to apply, end of Nov 2025 submitted application, mid Jan 2026 submitted application for L4E fellowship. Early Feb 2026 I get a Whatsapp message from my proposed secondary supervisor on a Sunday afternoon (Montreal time) asking if I'm available in the next couple of hours to discuss my application. As an international applicant in a different time zone unfortunately I was already asleep so replied first thing on Monday morning trying to arrange a time we could talk, and was told they would get back to me with a different time. The next thing I hear is on the 21st April when I get sent an email to look at the application portal where I find a generic rejection message. In the mean time I sent numerous follow up messages asking if they still wanted to talk with me but I never got a reply. McGill's website suggested that most applicants would hear back at the end of February and throughout March so towards the end of March I began to reach out by email to the proposed primary supervisor, program administrator, and L4E to see if they could give me any insight into the progress of my application or when I could expect to hear back. These emails and subsequent follow ups were also all completely ignored. I am obviously gutted about my application being rejected however given the seeming distinct lack of compassion, communication, and organisation shown by the anthropology department at McGill and the L4E it raises some major red flags to me about the quality of teaching and support that is offered by both the program and the fellowship. I would be very interested to hear from successful applicants about if this is the case? If the other applications I am still waiting on are also unsuccessful I will be applying for PhD programs again next year, however given the inadequacy of my experience this year I shan't be reapplying to McGill. Very disappointed.

comments: I had a very disappointing experience applying to the PhD program in EECS at the University of Wyoming. I submitted my application in January and never received any clear communication regarding its completeness. There were no notifications about missing documents, and every time I reached out for a status update, I received vague or delayed responses. In several instances, there was no reply at all. The lack of professionalism from the department, including the Graduate Coordinator, was frustrating. As an applicant investing significant time, effort, and money into the process, I expected at least basic transparency and communication. Unfortunately, that standard was not met. What makes this worse is that the final rejection cited multiple concerns, but none of these were ever communicated earlier in the process, nor was there any opportunity to clarify or strengthen the application. It raises serious questions about how thoroughly applications are handled and whether they are reviewed in a timely and organized manner. Overall, the experience felt disorganized, dismissive, and disrespectful toward applicants. Based on this experience, I would strongly caution prospective students to think carefully before applying here. Applicants deserve timely communication, clear guidance, and professional treatment—none of which I experienced in this process.

comments: Canadian domestic student. Applied in early March; notified by the end of March. Also note: "The University of Western Ontario" is also known as "Western University." Additional notes: I already went to graduate school here (finished with an MSc in Industrial-Organizational Psychology in the past). I completed some additional coursework (enough to warrant a second bachelor's degree in Math) and this is what the 3.60 (standardized GPA that takes into account institution) is based on. My grade average (as calculated by the school) was an 84%, somehow (I'm not sure how they arrived at this number; I think that even including only my last two years would have resulted in an average of 83.5% so maybe they rounded?). Every course on this transcript was a math, statistics, or computer science course (only one course from computer science; everything else was a roughly even split of math or statistics). I also had three summer research internships in Math and Statistics. I did not include any GRE scores because I did not include these in my application, but if anyone's curious, my old scores (back when I got into grad school the first time) were 94th percentile analytical writing, 97th percentile verbal, and 89th percentile quantitative (and I think that's because during that year, if you got perfect, it would still only be 94th percentile because of how many people would get perfect on that section). I also had prior experience with my selected supervisor (i.e., I attended his class and worked with him for one of my summer research internships).

First notification was in the portal with a two sentence rejection notice. Several days later I received an email with a more detailed explanation:  

"The Graduate Admissions Committee in the Department of English at the University of Florida has completed its review of applications and, unfortunately, has not selected you for admission.
 
This is no reflection on your academic excellence. We received more than 200 applications from talented and accomplished students all over the world for our graduate program, and we have admitted fewer than 10%. With so many excellent applicants to choose from, our decisions often came down to judgments about which students we can best support with our particular faculty expertise, our library resources, and the teaching and other training opportunities we can provide. Many of those who applied to our program can, we believe, actually be served better elsewhere. We hope that you get that opportunity, and we wish you luck and success in your future endeavors.
 
One final note: because we had so many applicants, we are unable to offer each applicant a detailed response on our Admissions Committee’s decision. Thank you for considering the University of Florida and for giving us an opportunity to review your materials. We are always amazed and humbled by the astonishing work that applicants to our program intend to do in the future. This year is no exception."

After a thorough and careful review of all materials by our Admissions Committee, I regret to inform you that we are unable to offer you a position in the program for the upcoming academic year.

This year, we received an exceptionally high number of applications from many talented individuals worldwide. Because our program is small and highly specialized, we are forced to make very difficult decisions, often turning down outstanding candidates due to the limited number of available spots and the specific alignment with our current research areas.

Please be assured that this decision is a result of the competitive nature of this year's pool and does not diminish your academic achievements or your potential for success in doctoral studies.

We are grateful for the opportunity to have considered your candidacy and wish you the very best in your academic journey and in all your future professional endeavors.

Best regards,

Davide Debortoli

The number of admission offers available at Princeton for entering graduate students is extremely limited, and we cannot offer admission to all applicants who are well qualified. Indeed, many departments have applicants who could be admitted if it were possible to accommodate additional students. Our decisions take into account not only the applicants’ merits but also the suitability of the programs to the candidates’ expressed interests. Our goal is to achieve a sound match between the strengths of our programs and the interests of the relatively small number of outstanding students that can be accommodated.

Unfortunately, due to the volume of applications which we receive, it is not possible for the department or the Graduate School to go back and review applications to justify the denial or offer advice on fortifying a future application.

I wish you success in your plans for graduate study and thank you for considering Princeton University."

comments: I presume it's a rejection, anyway, because surely "hmm we're struggling to figure out how to make the system display the details ... check tomorrow" is not what they'd choose for acceptances and waitlists.  I feel for the person I'm in email contact with, who sounds unsupported in their job (which perhaps also happened in 2024 if you look back in these results?).  I emailed asking when I might get my decision because it seems late.  They emailed back very promptly saying it should be in the portal.  I responded that when I log in to ApplyWeb, on the page where I can see all the universities that used ApplyWeb, there is a "decision letter" button above the "checklist" button but this doesn't appear for Cornell.  They responded that perhaps it needs to process overnight, but let them know if I still didn't see it tomorrow.  I talked to the tech support bot which suggests (Interesting to know!) that universities load a bunch of decision letters and then have to add a date and time and give permission for the student to view it (so if the college says it's there and I say it's not, they probably didn't give permission yet).  I sent that info to the kind administrative person at Cornell's History Graduate program, who thanked me for it and said it gave them an idea of a few things to go check.  Sounds like the funding cuts really hit a lot of areas -- my home department has had a lot of cuts and it's our admin person who is bearing the brunt of a lot of it.  Anyway.  Still can't see a decision in the portal, but it's apparent my application is just an administrative loose end, and this cycle has taught me that my research niche is "weird" and difficult for programs to find space for.  1a/7r/3p is I think the current tally, one pending is a Public Policy program.

"Thank you for your email and continued interest in UConn’s MA program. At this time, we have issued offers of acceptance to a very small number of applicants, as well as notifications to a few others that they have been placed on a selective waitlist. It is unlikely that we will move beyond our waitlist this year. Official decisions for all remaining applicants will likely be released after the April 15th deadline, as UConn adheres to the Council of Graduate Schools’ (CGS) “April 15 Resolution”: April 15 Resolution - CGS (cgsnet.org). Applicants who have received offers have until April 15th to respond."

When making admissions decisions we consider the applicant's academic record, type and range of teaching and professional experiences, and specified research interests. In addition to selecting only those applicants with top ratings in all of these categories, we look for those whose research interests closely match the scholarly expertise of the APLNG faculty. Thus, each year we reject applicants with strong applications but with research interests that are not the best fit with our faculty.  This year, the decisions were particularly difficult as we had a large number of highly qualified applicants.

"...Applying to graduate school takes significant energy and time, and we were honored that you included us among your choices for application. While we aren’t able to offer specific feedback on your application, please know that our decision this year is not a negative evaluation of your suitability for graduate school or a career in the history profession. Each year, we must forego the opportunity to work with and learn from many talented applicants. The loss is entirely ours, and we hope that you will find another path where you will be supported to pursue your passions."

Our decisions about admission should therefore not be taken as a judgment about your overall potential for graduate study. Many who are refused here go elsewhere and do superbly.
